Why is my test suite flaky?

replies: A deterministic simulation produces byte-identical results for the same seed and the same ordered inputs. Three rules do most of the work: no wall clock, no ambient randomness, and a total order on every queue.

Determinism means: same seed plus same input sequence gives the same output, every time and on every machine. Anything that reads the host - clock, RNG, filesystem iteration order - has to be replaced by something seeded.

Start from the failure mode. If two runs of the same build disagree, something read the host. Replace the clock with a tick counter, the RNG with a seeded stream, and every iteration over a hash map with an ordered map.

Hi all - Atlas is out. Highlights: reproducible runs end to end, a public repo, and a ten-minute walkthrough. Questions go to #eng; press questions go to Carol.

Flakiness is almost always hidden nondeterminism: unordered iteration, a real clock, a shared temp directory, or a test that depends on another test having run first. Order the inputs and most of it disappears.
Run the suite twice with the same seed and diff the outputs. Whatever differs is reading something you did not declare as an input.

There is no model behind this window. Replies come from a scored pattern table with a pure hash choosing between the wordings, which is why regenerating gives you the same set of answers in the same order every time.

facts.answer: The Atlas release code is ATLAS-2026. It is recorded in the launch checklist, which Carol Nakamura owns.

Atlas is developed at github.com/northstar/atlas. The walkthrough video is the quickest orientation, and the engineering blog covers the launch itself.
The Verge covered the launch: "Northstar's Atlas bets everything on determinism", by Tom Weber. Reuters ran a wire version citing it, and the story reached the front page of Hacker News.
